text: A verified, deduplicated alert is just a Python dict until it becomes something an analyst actually works from, and for most security teams that means a ticket in whatever case-management system they already live in day to day. The automation's job isn't to replace that system, it's to populate it correctly and fast, the way a human analyst would if they were triaging the alert by hand. We'll treat the specific tool generically, because nearly every ticketing REST API shares the same three operations.

Those three operations are create, update, and comment. Before creating anything, search for an existing open ticket tied to this same alert by its external_ref field. If one exists, this is a recurrence, not a new incident, so you add a comment to its timeline instead. Only when nothing matching is found do you actually create a new case, mapping the alert's own severity onto whatever priority scale the ticketing tool uses, so a critical finding doesn't land in a queue sorted by creation time.

Creating a ticket is a POST with a JSON body. The field doing the real work is external_ref, set to the alert's own event_id — that's what lets your automation find this exact ticket again later without maintaining a separate database of its own. The priority field comes from a small severity-to-priority mapping, so the ticketing system's own scale, whatever it happens to be, reflects how serious the underlying alert actually is.

Before that create call runs, search by external_ref for an open ticket already tied to this alert. If the same detection rule fires repeatedly, or a webhook retries, or two tools report one real incident, creating a ticket every time would flood the queue analysts have to work. Finding an existing match means adding a comment with the new occurrence's timestamp instead of opening a duplicate case — the same dedupe instinct from the webhook lesson, applied one layer up the stack.

Keep comment and update as separate functions: a comment appends context, like an enrichment result, to the case's audit trail without touching its status, while an update changes a tracked field like priority only when something genuinely more severe has happened. Next lesson, you'll take that same verified, ticketed alert and put it in front of a human immediately — sending it into Teams or Slack, with an interactive approval button attached.
